title: Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Industrial Fault Diagnosis and Prognostics: Evidence, Applicability Boundaries, and a Practical Deployment Guide
abstract: Data-driven fault diagnosis is held back mainly by scarce labelled fault data. Faults are rare, operating regimes differ, and each new task needs its own training. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) such as TabPFN promise a way around this: pretrained once on synthetic tasks, they predict for a new machine from a small labelled context without retraining. This review tests that promise for industrial fault diagnosis and prognostics, combining a reproducible scoping review of applications with experiments on a synthetic problem with known optima and on a public bearing benchmark. The benchmark is split temporally within each recording, which still shares recordings between context and test data, and, more strictly, across operating loads. The evidence supports a benefit for tabular data with few labelled faults, but its size depends on operating conditions and reference models. On the bearing data, the margin over the strongest tree ensembles was small within one load and vanished across loads. Tuned tree ensembles remain preferable under changing conditions, tight latency budgets and plentiful labels, and the evidence on imbalance, calibration and drift is still thin. The article provides a decision roadmap, open reference code, a reporting checklist and an operating model for PFN-based diagnosers.
title_zh: Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Industrial Fault Diagnosis and Prognostics: Evidence, Applicability Boundaries, and a Practical Deployment Guide

title: Observer-Based Fault Diagnosis and Fault-Tolerant Control of DC-DC Converters in Photovoltaic Systems: A Critical Review with Emphasis on Sliding Mode Techniques
abstract: DC-DC converters that interface photovoltaic (PV) generators with loads, batteries or inverters are highly stressed, and their faults directly reduce energy yield. This review examines fault diagnosis and fault-tolerant control (FTC) of PV DC-DC converters, with emphasis on observer-based and sliding mode techniques. Literature published between 2015 and 2026 was identified on five scholarly platforms and by citation tracking; 40 primary studies were classified and compared against 13 features, including fault coverage, detection speed, fault estimation, robustness to maximum power point tracking (MPPT) and irradiance transients, sensor needs, computational load and validation level. Two-thirds were published since 2021. Switch faults dominate (25 studies), whereas sensor (11) and component faults (6) receive less attention; 14 studies implement an FTC action, and 11 report experimental validation. Sliding mode observers form the largest and fastest-growing family (14 studies, 13 since 2021) and combine robustness with fault reconstruction, but experimental results are reported for only one of them, on a PV inverter. A framework linking fault classes, diagnosis information, FTC strategies and reaction times is proposed, with a design procedure and a combined-uncertainty validation protocol. Closing the loop between model-based diagnosis and FTC under realistic PV conditions remains the main open need.
title_zh: Observer-Based Fault Diagnosis and Fault-Tolerant Control of DC-DC Converters in Photovoltaic Systems: A Critical Review with Emphasis on Sliding Mode Techniques

title: Data-driven predictive control of battery energy storage with physics-informed sequence modeling
abstract: Integrating battery energy storage systems (BESS) into industrial sites with photovoltaic generation and time-varying tariffs requires controllers that combine economic performance, low real-time computational cost, and robustness to forecast errors. Model predictive control (MPC) achieves near-optimal cost but solves a mixed-integer optimization at every step using a linearized battery model, since nonlinear formulations are intractable for real-time deployment. Learning-based controllers remove this online optimization, but they are typically trained without any knowledge of the equipment they operate on; they are tuned site by site, and they provide no structural guarantee that operational constraints will be met. Closing this gap is the motivation of this work. This paper proposes PI-DT, a data-driven predictive controller based on a transformer sequence model conditioned on the return-to-go, trained offline on linear MILP expert actions executed on a nonlinear Thévenin two-branch RC battery simulator, and informed by per-battery physics, so that a single network operates batteries of different capacity, rated power, and efficiency without per-site retraining. An asymmetric minimum terminal state of charge (SOC) constraint, closer to industrial practice than a fixed target, is enforced consistently across expert, MPC, and the proposed controller, and enforced at inference through a horizon-aware projection on the action. The evaluation uses the public EMSx dataset (60 industrial sites, 37,442 site-days, Spanish PVPC tariff) and compares against the Rolling MPC, behavior cloning (BC), and Implicit Q-Learning (IQL), all assessed under the same nonlinear battery dynamics. On 5577 test site-days, the proposed controller reaches an aggregate cost gap of 1.39% versus the MILP, below 1.54% (BC), 1.61% (MPC), and 1.96% (IQL). The learning baselines fall below the minimum terminal SOC by up to 8.4 and 29 percentage points, respectively; the projection makes the reserve feasible by construction under the linear SOC model on which it is computed, and on the nonlinear plant the worst-case residual deficit of the proposed controller is 0.14 pp, within the 1 pp operational tolerance. A 3-fold cross-validation on held-out sites shows it transfers to unseen batteries with negligible degradation. The proposed controller therefore attains MPC-level economics without an online solver and with a structurally enforced end-of-day reserve, which makes it a candidate for embedded deployment in industrial energy management systems, subject to hardware-in-the-loop validation.

title: Quantifying non-uniform geometric changes in an aged prismatic battery module using X-ray computed tomography
abstract: Swelling in lithium-ion cells can translate into non-uniform deformation inside mechanically constrained multi-cell assemblies, but quantitative, spatially resolved characterization at the assembly scale remains limited. Here, we present an X-ray computed tomography (CT)-based workflow to quantify aging-induced geometric change and geometric inhomogeneity in an 8-cell prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) module operated under mechanical constraint. The module was scanned at the beginning of life and in an aged state, corresponding to a module state of health of 86.58% based on discharge capacity, under matched conditions of 30% module-level state of charge and 25 °C. From the reconstructed CT volumes, spatial fields of cell thickness and inter-cell gaps were extracted using an edge-based image-processing workflow and summarized using statistical descriptors (mean, standard deviation, interquartile range). After cycling, all cells exhibited net thickening and all inter-cell gaps decreased, while the overall stack thickness changed only marginally, indicating that swelling was largely accommodated by compression of the inter-cell pads. The thickness-distribution descriptors further indicated tendencies toward increased within-cell heterogeneity and cell-to-cell dispersion. The cell-to-cell geometric differences were accompanied by greater electrochemical dispersion in the aged-state capacity determination test. The proposed workflow provides non-destructive, spatially resolved metrics for evaluating deformation accommodation in constrained battery stacks and for generating quantitative reference data for model validation and design assessment.
title_zh: Quantifying non-uniform geometric changes in an aged prismatic battery module using X-ray computed tomography
